study.title: Galatians 2 - The gospel preserved by grace, not by the Law
study.overview: In this chapter, Paul narrates two decisive scenes to defend the integrity of the gospel he preaches. First, he shows that his message to the Gentiles was recognized by the leaders of Jerusalem, without Titus being forced to circumcise himself. He then reports his public confrontation with Peter in Antioch, when he realized that Peter's practice contradicted the truth of the gospel. The chapter culminates in the central affirmation that no one is justified by the works of the Law, but by faith in Jesus Christ; therefore, to return to the Law would be to nullify the grace of God and treat the death of Christ as something without need.

outline.title: The trip to Jerusalem and the defense of freedom in Christ
outline.explanation: Paul says that he went up by revelation, presented his gospel in particular, and did not allow Titus to be constrained to circumcision. The concern was not to seek human validation, but to preserve the truth of the gospel against the false brothers who wanted to turn Christian freedom into slavery.

outline.title: Mutual recognition and unity between missions
outline.explanation: The leaders considered columns recognized the grace given to Paul and Barnabas, realizing that the same God acted on different fronts: Peter between the circumcised and Paul among the Gentiles. Communion was sealed with the right hand and accompanied by the practical commitment to remember the poor.

outline.title: Rebuke Peter and the Doctrine of Justification by Faith
outline.explanation: When Peter retreated for fear of the circumcision group, Paul publicly corrected him because his conduct denied the truth of the gospel in practice. Then Paul declares that Jews and Gentiles are justified only by faith in Christ; if righteousness came by the Law, then Christ would have died uselessly.

study.context: The chapter reflects real tensions in the early church between Christians of Jewish origin and of Gentile origin. The notes indicate that Paul describes a previous visit to Jerusalem and not necessarily the later council, although there is a discussion amongst commentators about this identification. The text also shows Antioch as a place where the coexistence between Christian Jews and Gentiles made visible the dispute between maintaining Jewish practices and preserving the freedom of the gospel.
study.theology: The theological thesis of the chapter is that the grace of God in Christ is sufficient to justify the human being; it does not depend on the works of the Law. Circumcision, ethnic distinctions, and ceremonial customs cannot be imposed as a condition of acceptance before God. Faith in Christ unites Jews and Gentiles in the same salvation, and any attempt to add the Law as the basis of righteousness contradicts the gospel. Moreover, Christian life is born of a union with Christ: the believer is crucified with him and lives by faith in the Son of God, so that the cross is not a complement, but the foundation of salvation.

scholarViews.insight: Paul presented his gospel in particular to the leaders of Jerusalem not to seek human approval, but to preserve the unity of the church between Jews and Gentiles and avoid division.
Peter's reaction in Antioch shows that even an apostle could act in an incoherent manner by human fear; therefore Paul rebuked him to protect the truth of the gospel.
If righteousness came by observance of the Law, then the death of Christ would be without purpose; the conclusion of the apostle is that justification is not of the Law, but by faith in Christ.

questions: In what situations can I be accepting, in practice, a religious or social pressure that contradicts the freedom of the gospel?
Have I treated God's grace as sufficient for my justification, or do I try to add merits, rites or moral performance as a basis for acceptance before God?
My attitudes in public correspond to the truth that I confess to believe?
study.practice: Examine your life in the light of the coherence between belief and practice. Reject every attempt to transform symbols, habits, or rules into a condition of acceptance by God. Long live unity with other brothers without despising secondary differences, but without yielding into central gospel principles. Also practice the remembrance of the needy, as a concrete sign of Christian communion, and try to correct with meekness what is in disagreement with the truth of Christ.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not allow to state with certainty whether the visit of Galatians 2 corresponds to the council of Acts 15 or a previous visit; therefore this identification should remain as an interpretative possibility, not as established fact. Nor is it possible to determine with absolute certainty, from the given notes, what specific revelation motivated Paul's ascent to Jerusalem.
